raw_text: {"translation": "The need for drugs arises for human beings often simply as this alone, namely of drugs that either heat or cool or moisten or dry, or that act according to some conjunction of these; but sometimes as of drugs that tighten and draw together what has already been relaxed beyond the limit of the moderate, [707] or relax what is tensed, or rarefy what has been condensed or condense what is loose, or soften what is hard or harden immoderate softnesses, or empty what is full or fill what is empty, or that accomplish some other such thing. For one who has been chilled—not only a physician, but any layman whatever—led by the very nature of the matter, desires to find a heating drug, and likewise one who is being burnt up by a burning fever desires a cooling one. So too any layman whatever who has a sodden ulcer bids the physician to dry it, and, if it should be dry and moistureless, to moisten it. And indeed, when they perceive dryness together with heat throughout the whole body, as do both those who have been scorched by the sun and those who have been worn out by fatigue, they long to bathe and they drink cold water, and whatever may be capable of moistening and cooling at once, this they contrive to find out; and many of the laymen, led by nature itself, often procure for themselves the remedies for these conditions.", "renderings": [{"target_no": 51, "surface": "μανὸν,", "english": "what is loose", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 58, "surface": "ἀμέτρους", "english": "immoderate", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 63, "surface": "πλῆρες", "english": "what is full", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 93, "surface": "θερμαῖνον", "english": "heating", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 100, "surface": "ἐμψῦχον.", "english": "cooling one", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 112, "surface": "ἰατρὸν", "english": "physician", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 119, "surface": "ἄνικμον,", "english": "moistureless", "uncertain": "n"}, {"target_no": 176, "surface": "ἰάματα.", "english": "remedies", "uncertain": "n"}], "uncertain_greek": ["ὡς ἤδη τὸ πέρας τοῦ μετρίου κεχαλασμένον"]}

raw_text: {"translation": "Concerning such matters of power, then, I have gone through in the four treatises before this one: in the first and second, refuting the arguments of the sophists and showing the true method by using which one might find the powers of drugs; in the third, having taken leave of the sophists, I went through from the beginning all the logical inquiries, by going through which especially, and being, as one might say, trained by them, one will be capable of finding the powers of all drugs; and in the fourth I made my discourse about the objects of sense proper to the [710] tongue, which indeed they name flavours (χυμοί), demonstrating how one, setting out from there, might find the primary qualities and powers. I also touched, to the extent that need called for it, on the odorous qualities at the end of that book, showing how much it is possible to take from there too for the discovery of the primary powers. But in this present discourse, the fifth, another kind of powers is set before me to expound—second, as one might say, and third, after the primary ones that are common to all. raw_text: {"translation": "But because it seemed good to me to train in advance those who are going to follow the reasonings of the therapeutic method, and because most of my companions, and especially [714] those to gratify whom I came to this treatise, asked me to carry it through in this way, for this reason I shall take up the discussion in this book, making my beginning from the suppurating and the softening drugs; since both are hot and moist, yet each in a different manner. raw_text: {"translation": "For at present it is not my purpose to go through all the material, but to produce one general teaching concerning all such powers—namely, what the general point is which it is better to know about both the suppurating and the softening agents: that the former kindle a heat equal to that of the animal according to nature, whereas those that soften kindle much more; and that the former by nature act not by the quality of the heat but rather by its quantity, whereas those that are softening of indurated parts [729] act rather by the quality. raw_text: {"translation": "But we must not misunderstand him, and must recognize that 'innate heat' has been said of that which we also call pneuma in each of the animals, about [731] which Aristotle too wrote. And nothing prevents one from understanding by 'innate heat' also the blood-like and airy substance together with the pneuma. Now the Stoics hold that this very pneuma is the substance of the soul; but we neither venture at all to pronounce on the substance of the soul, and we consider it superfluous for the present purpose. That, however, the innate pneuma, even if it is not the substance of the soul, is at any rate its first instrument, we have already demonstrated in the commentaries On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato. And indeed we say that this pneuma is contained in all the parts of the animal, but that it is not alike everywhere, just as it is not necessary that the blood be either. raw_text: {"translation": "Hence also mandrake and hemlock, henbane and poppy—I mean now the herbs themselves—if one uses them moderately, are condensing [752] in their powers; if more, they are not only condensing but already also numbing; and if to the greatest degree, they are no longer only numbing but already also mortifying. raw_text: {"translation": "For among things that are similar in their substances, the hotter is more drawing, [761] inasmuch as it has taken on heat as an ally to the similarity. For such a thing, drawing by two causes, will have the advantage over that which attracts by only one of them. And it will make no difference whether one speaks of an attractive (epispastikē), a drawing (helktikē) or a drawing-in (helkystikē) power. But since enough has been said about these too, let us pass on to the powers named alexeterial and alexipharmic. The nature of these too is twofold: some alter, while others evacuate from the affected body either the destructive venom or the deleterious drug. Their powers are most opposite to one another. For some are of a thinning nature, others of a thickening one. The thinning power, then, arises in hot and fine-particled substances, the thickening in cold and coarse-particled ones. Let this discussion, then, end here. It is fitting to pass on to the one deferred a little earlier.

raw_text: {"translation": "But that which is either drier or moister, or hotter [787] or colder, is named from the predominating power. So too cold and moist and dry, whatever requires demonstration, not yet having acquired a strong or manifest activity. Those things, however, that are already of such a nature as to heat or cool or dry or moisten clearly will be said to be of the second order. Those that do so already vehemently, yet not to the extreme, of the third. And those that are of such a nature as to heat so as both to form an eschar and to burn, of the fourth. So likewise those that are of such a nature as to cool more vehemently, so as already to mortify, these too are of the fourth. raw_text: {"translation": "For that the tongue is by nature capable of discerning a dry and a wet and a hot and a cold body no less than all the other parts of the animal [621] is obvious to everyone; but bitternesses and sweetnesses, saltinesses and sournesses, harshnesses and acerbities and pungencies, it alone is believed to distinguish, although the similarity of the affections can be found in all the other parts as well, and especially in those that are ulcerated. raw_text: {"translation": "For we have experienced something of this sort also in the case of vinegar: being unable to see its generation through sense-perception, we disbelieve the argument. raw_text: {"translation": "These points, then, are sufficiently in agreement with one another — both what has been said on the basis of the very substance of the things and what has been said by way of induction from what is discovered by perception. But it would be no worse to add these points too, recalling here again the usage of the names: that both are said to be astringent, the harsh and the acerbic, but they differ in the more [640] and the less. And indeed, that drugs possess many qualities, not only different but also in conflict with one another, and sometimes even wholly opposed, has been sufficiently shown before; but it is necessary now too to begin from this point. For if, when you taste it, the same thing appears to you to be at once both acerbic and biting, I shall bid you leave this drug aside and go on to the one that is acerbic without being biting. response.translation: And for this reason the things that chill us completely and deaden us, such as hemlock and poppy-juice (meconium), henbane and mandrake, are least of all [667] sour. All the sour flavours are indeed cold, yet they do not cool to such a degree as to kill. One tests it, as to what sort of thing it is in its nature, in the case of oxylapathon and oxalis, which indeed they also call oxys. This is a wild pot-herb; for in these it appeared to me to be, in some way, most unadulterated and alone, sharing in no acerbity, as the fruits of trees do. For these manifestly have their sourness mixed with some acerbity, just as vinegar has it mixed with pungency. Now what is properly named sour among the flavours is perceptible to the tongue alone, as is also the pungent. But what is common to both, the biting, is already perceptible also to touch. And the tongue is capable of discerning both: the common ones, as any other of the sentient bodies is too; the proper ones, as the organ of taste. And it seems to me that this special property belongs to it in accordance with the kinship and the alienness of whole substances.

raw_text: {"translation": "At any rate, when sweet things are heated further, whether [686] by fire or by the innate heat, the generation of bitter bodies was shown to take place. And straightaway these appear drier in their consistency, and, because their moisture is continually being consumed and flowing away, vaporised by the heat, it is necessary that what is left behind be rendered more earthy and drier. For the sweet itself, in addition to being hot to a greater or lesser degree, is surely of necessity also moist to a greater or lesser degree. For the salty flavour is near to the bitter, since both are earthy and hot; yet they differ by no obscure difference, in that the bitter has been thinned and worked up more by dry heat. So too, of the salts themselves, those that are harder and denser and more earthy—and such are almost all the mined salts—are less hot and fine-particled, whereas those that are friable and loose-textured are at once both more fine-particled and hotter in power, and some of them are somewhat bitter, being in a way intermediate between the hard salts and aphronitron. There are indeed also some of the aphronitra themselves that are hard and coarse-particled, and do not even dissolve easily in water.

raw_text: {"translation": "For in the relative sense it is very easy, when one comes to the particular cases, to say that rose oil, when applied to such-and-such a body, is of a nature to preserve it in the mixture in which it found it, whereas when brought to another body of such-and-such a kind it heats [570] and another it cools. But to make a universal pronouncement about its power is difficult without first drawing distinctions and reaching an agreement about the names. raw_text: {"translation": "[579] For if there were always a single quality in each of the drugs that are astringent to the taste, it would never be the case that some of them are edible and others drug-like; rather, they would differ from one another only in being more or less astringent. But as things are, this is not so. For one kind of astringency appears pleasant and agreeable, another unpleasant and drug-like: that of pear, apple and pomegranate pleasant, that of scale of copper and aloe unpleasant and drug-like. And yet scale of copper is less astringent than a quince-apple, so that one could not even refer the strangeness of its quality to the vehemence of its astringency. raw_text: {"translation": "For it has already been shown many times that all the qualities act upon one another in some respect, and that a stone has been affected by the continuous striking of a drip of water, and a sword has been blunted while cutting wax; and it has further been demonstrated that the activities in animals come about through the solid bodies within them, so that so long as these have not yet been chilled by the cooling drugs, it is necessary [598] that the animal survive; but they are not chilled before the drugs have penetrated into their proper pores. And this does not belong of themselves to the coarse-grained and cold drugs, unless they happen upon something to guide them. What guides them, as the first cause, is the attraction of the arteries, for these were shown, in dilating, to draw everything that lies near; and, as the second and material cause, the fineness of parts of the substance, which the colder and more coarse-particled drugs, not possessing it of themselves, need others to supply. Accordingly, all bodies that are cold in their mixtures both have the attraction of the arteries weaker than hot ones—for this too was shown—and are unable quickly to break down the substances of the drugs into small parts. response.translation: For it has already been shown many times that all the qualities act upon one another in some respect, and that a stone has been affected by the continuous striking of a drip of water, and a sword has been blunted while cutting wax; and it has further been demonstrated that the activities in animals come about through the solid bodies within them, so that so long as these have not yet been chilled by the cooling drugs, it is necessary [598] that the animal survive; but they are not chilled before the drugs have penetrated into their proper pores. And this does not belong of themselves to the coarse-grained and cold drugs, unless they happen upon something to guide them. What guides them, as the first cause, is the attraction of the arteries, for these were shown, in dilating, to draw everything that lies near; and, as the second and material cause, the fineness of parts of the substance, which the colder and more coarse-particled drugs, not possessing it of themselves, need others to supply. Accordingly, all bodies that are cold in their mixtures both have the attraction of the arteries weaker than hot ones—for this too was shown—and are unable quickly to break down the substances of the drugs into small parts. And in consequence the drug, delaying, is itself likely to undergo something in the course of time, so that sometimes it is even concocted; just as the juice of lettuce also is. For in time this too is concocted; but if it manages to reach the heart unimpaired, it kills much like hemlock. And all the other strongly cooling juices undergo this as well.

raw_text: {"translation": "And indeed, [617] if it is purgative of black bile, it will evacuate that first, and after it the yellow, then in the same way the phlegm, and last of all the blood will follow, as though flowing out from vessels that are by now lifeless, since great weakness has seized them and their mouths have arrived at extreme distension. raw_text: {"translation": "For not even knowing why white hellebore purges upward and black downward, [477] nor knowing why cnecus is evacuative of phlegm and epithymum of black humours, they nevertheless use the drugs for those purposes which experience has taught, and they treat those in need, and they trust what is evidently apparent, and they laugh at those who establish the contrary by reasoning. But Archidamus, in addition to his disdaining, in many matters, what is evidently apparent, seems to me to deserve justly to be censured in this respect as well. response.translation: For not even knowing why white hellebore purges upward and black downward, [477] nor knowing why cnecus is evacuative of phlegm and epithymum of black humours, they nevertheless use the drugs for those purposes which experience has taught, and they treat those in need, and they trust what is evidently apparent, and they laugh at those who establish the contrary by reasoning. raw_text: {"translation": "[505] For they guard against the greater heat, which alters it in quality and readily gives it a burnt, greasy smell; or they set olive-stones or grain around it in a circle, or they add certain drugs to the vessels themselves; in a word, they draw out and consume the watery part and preserve what remains. raw_text: {"translation": "The sources of this kind of dispute are three: the failure to distinguish the kinds of things that are said to heat [524] us, the confused use of homonymies, and the failure to leave room for any mean. And as for 'the hot' itself, we are accustomed to name thus both what is already such in actuality and what is so in potentiality, as has often been said before as well. But that which is hot in actuality includes both what is hot simply, like fire, and what is hot by predominance, like the animal, and what is hot when compared with the well-proportioned member of the same genus, and what is hot relative to anything whatever that happens to be at hand. raw_text: {"translation": "[382] First, then, and above all, one must make the test of the power under judgement on the basis of the very thing in relation to which it is predicated. For it does not follow, if hemlock is cooling for a human being, that it is thereby so also for a starling, nor, if it is nourishing for a starling (ἀνθρώπων), that it is thereby so also for a human being. In the same way, it does not follow, if hellebore is purgative, that it is thereby so also for quails, nor, if it is nourishing for them, that it is thereby so also for human beings. Next, one must distinguish what is so per accidens from what is so primarily and in virtue of itself. For cold water sometimes produces a recalling of heat by cooling the skin and contracting and condensing it; for a recalling of heat follows upon this, as was shown in the third book On Mixtures. Hot, in turn, often cools by dispersing the humour that is doing the heating. raw_text: {"translation": "But to make the judgement from nothing other than that in relation to which the power is predicated is actually quite easy: we are to examine neither whether oil is destructive of insects, nor whether it is [383] oily or viscous or light, when what we are inquiring into is whether it is of a nature to heat, or to cool, or to dry, or to moisten the human body. In the same way, we are to examine neither whether the rose is red in colour, nor whether white lead is white. For neither is what is red necessarily hot nor what is white necessarily cold; rather, the question is whether, when applied to our bodies, they heat them primarily and in themselves, and neither through some other intermediary nor incidentally; and if this be so (εἴη), then they are hot in power, just as, if they cool, they are cold. raw_text: {"translation": "The one of the principles — or lemmas, or [402] axioms, or premises, or however you may wish to name them — that go into the demonstration has been demonstrated in the commentaries On Mixtures: that the whole skin is continuous with itself in its original generation, but in time becomes perforated and has very many pores, in the same way as sieves. raw_text: {"translation": "And in the same way, too, whichever of them appears more or less [411] hard, this must necessarily turn out in proportion to the magnitude of the excess. One must therefore bear these things in mind, and also that being cooled is not the same thing as being congealed, even if the latter comes about most of all through being cooled. For being cooled is receiving a cold quality, whereas being congealed is being hardened through cooling. And at this one might well wonder at those who have investigated such things, seeing them fall by their own hands in most of the matters they investigate and write about, like Herodotus. For beginning from the whole most ancient record of compound drugs, they proceed to the examination of the simples contained in them: since vinegar, say, has been mixed into these particular heating drugs, on that basis they straightway declare that it too is hot. For it is reasonable, I think, that what has been combined with something that is in its mixture neither of the extremes but, as far as possible, intermediate should itself be the cause of the effects produced. response.translation: For these very reasons, then, and because many of my companions wished that the fallacies of the more recent physicians be refuted, not only in the gatherings which we hold on each occasion when spending time together with them, but also through these commentaries, I was compelled to linger at greater length over the first two books, so that in the third, having by then a hearer pure in soul and able to follow true arguments, I may go through all that one must know about the principles of the [458] inquiry set before us, and after that go through all the powers of each of the drugs. Since it now has its due measure, I set this sentence upon it as its conclusion.
